title: Access methods
lead: Sequential scans, composite search keys, index-only scans and bitmap access.

sections.title: Sequential scans and index selection
sections.html:
An access path retrieves base-table tuples and applies applicable predicates. A sequential scan reads every table page and checks its tuples. For N pages its read cost is N even if only a small fraction of tuples qualifies.

Selectivity estimates output rows, not automatically source pages avoided. Reducing reads requires a suitable access path or metadata that can skip pages. A tree index supports equality and ranges; a hash index supports equality over its complete search key.

Choosing an index requires comparing its supported predicates, key uniqueness, clustering and matching-row count. Residual predicates still need to be checked after candidate records have been found.

PDF pp. 1–6

sections.title: Composite keys and lexicographic ranges
sections.html:
A tree index on (A₁, A₂, …) orders keys lexicographically. A conventional contiguous lookup uses equalities on a leading prefix and optionally a range on the next attribute. Later conditions can be residual filters without narrowing the entire scan into one smaller interval.

In the source index (Age, Salary), Age = 55 AND Salary > 200 forms a contiguous range. Age > 31 AND Salary = 400 does not form one exact lexicographic interval: other salary values occur between matches.

An index on (Age, Salary) therefore differs from one on (Salary, Age). Conditions without a leading-key bound may require a broad index scan or a specialised access strategy rather than a direct prefix lookup.

PDF pp. 7–15

sections.title: Index-only, clustered and hash scans
sections.html:
An index-only scan can answer a query from attributes stored in index entries, without fetching the required values from heap records. The source illustrates grouping by dno using an index on dno, and MIN(salary) per department using (dno, salary). Real engines may additionally need visibility checks.

Clustered scans retrieve matching records with good data-page locality. Unclustered scans can fetch many pages; sorting candidate RIDs by page can reduce repeated or random access. Counting matching index entries is different from counting distinct data pages.

A composite hash index requires equality values for the complete hashed key. A hash index on (age, dept) matches both values together; age alone does not identify its bucket.

PDF pp. 16–19

sections.title: Multi-index and bitmap scans
sections.html:
A multi-index path obtains candidate RID sets from several indexes. AND predicates generally intersect these sets; OR predicates can union sets when all relevant branches are represented. The engine fetches candidate records and checks residual predicates.

A bitmap represents candidate tuple positions or page locations compactly and can organise heap fetches by page. The PostgreSQL example separates Bitmap Index Scan, which constructs candidates, from Bitmap Heap Scan, which fetches records and rechecks conditions where required.

The source’s PostgreSQL exercise uses a Learn-provided dataset and EXPLAIN/EXPLAIN ANALYZE. Its restricted worksheet is not reproduced here. Access-path choice depends on table size, selectivity, available indexes and estimated cost.

PDF pp. 20–23

quiz.question: Which predicate forms a contiguous range in an index on (A,B)?
options: B=20 with any value of A
A>7 AND B=20 with no residual check needed at all
quiz.explanation: An equality prefix on A followed by a range on B forms one contiguous interval in the index.

source.summary: The complete official PDF was read. Topics covered: Sequential scan and selectivity; Index eligibility and key ordering; Composite B+ tree prefix/range rule; Index-only, clustered, unclustered scans; Hash composite equality; Multi-index RID intersection/union; PostgreSQL EXPLAIN practical scope. The explanations and calculations above are original teaching material, not reproductions of the slides.
